words.definition: something bad that happens by chance, often causing damage or injury

meet.sentence: There was a car {accident} near the school, but luckily nobody was hurt.

questions.prompt: something bad that happens by chance, often causing damage or injury

questions.sentence: I didn't mean to break your phone. It was an {_}!
He had a bike {accident} and broke his arm.
questions.explain: Correct. An accident is something bad that happens by chance.

questions.sentence: We had a great {accident} at the beach and swam all day.
questions.explain: An accident is something bad that happens by chance. A great time at the beach is a fun day.

questions.them: Why is your arm in a cast?? 😮
questions.me: I had a small {_} at basketball practice. I'll be fine!

questions.them: Did you spill juice on my notebook on purpose?!
questions.me: No! It was an {_}, I'm so sorry 😬

questions.sentence: I {_} deleted all my photos. Can I get them back?
questions.hint: You need an adverb that means 'by mistake'. Many adverbs end in -ly.

questions.sentence: I met my best friend by {_}: we sat next to each other on a bus.
questions.explain: 'By accident' means by chance, without planning it.

words.definition: to like and respect someone or something very much

meet.sentence: I really {admire} my grandmother: she raised five children and still found time to volunteer.

questions.prompt: to like and respect someone or something very much

questions.sentence: Many young players {_} Messi for his skill and hard work.
We stopped to {admire} the view from the top of the mountain.
questions.explain: Correct. You can admire a person, or something beautiful like a view.

questions.sentence: I {admired} the bus because I was late.
questions.explain: Admire means to like and respect. When you're late, you run to catch the bus.

questions.them: Who's your role model?
questions.me: My mom. I really {_} how hard she works ❤️

questions.them: Did you see Noa's drawing? It's incredible 🎨
questions.me: Yes! I {_} people who can draw like that.

questions.sentence: The firefighters' bravery filled everyone with {_}.
questions.hint: You need a noun. Many nouns end in -ation.

options.text: I {admire} her for being so honest.
Tourists stood and {admired} the old city walls.
He {admired} that he had taken the money.
She {admires} the floor every morning with a mop.

questions.explain: You admire a person or something beautiful. To say you did something wrong, you admit it. And you clean a floor.

words.definition: to agree that something is true, often something bad that you did

meet.sentence: Finally, Tom {admitted} that he had eaten the last piece of cake.

questions.prompt: to agree that something is true, often something bad that you did

questions.sentence: After the police showed him the video, the man {_} that he stole the bike.
I have to {admit} that your idea is better than mine.
questions.explain: Correct. Admit = agree that something is true, even if you don't want to.

questions.sentence: Can you {admit} the door? It's cold in here.
questions.explain: Admit means to agree that something is true. For a door, you close it.

questions.them: Wait, did you cheat in the game last night? 😂
questions.me: OK, OK, I {_} it! I looked at your cards 🙈

questions.them: Why are you so quiet? Is something wrong?
questions.me: I have to {_} something... I lost the book you lent me 😔

questions.sentence: Only people with a ticket will be {_} into the concert hall.
questions.explain: Admit can also mean 'let someone enter': to be admitted into a place.

words.definition: something that helps you or makes you better than others

meet.sentence: One {advantage} of living in a big city is that there's always something to do.

questions.prompt: something that helps you or makes you better than others

questions.sentence: Being tall is a big {_} in basketball.
Speaking two languages is a real {advantage} when you look for a job.
questions.explain: Correct. An advantage is something that helps you.

questions.sentence: I'm hungry. Can I have an {advantage} with cheese?
questions.explain: An advantage is something that helps you. With cheese, you'd ask for a sandwich or a toast.

questions.them: Why did you pick the school next to your house?
questions.me: The big {_} is that I can sleep until 7:45 😴

questions.them: Is it better to buy the phone online or at the store?
questions.me: Online has one {_}: it's 200 shekels cheaper.

questions.sentence: The only {_} of the trip is that we have to wake up at 5am.
questions.hint: You need the opposite of advantage. Add a beginning that means 'not'.

questions.sentence: Smart students take {_} of the free lessons after school.
questions.explain: 'Take advantage of something' means use a chance well.

words.definition: an exciting experience, sometimes a little dangerous

meet.sentence: Camping alone in the desert for three days was a real {adventure}.

questions.prompt: an exciting experience, sometimes a little dangerous

questions.sentence: The movie is about a boy's exciting {_} on a pirate ship.
Our trip to the Galilee was a great {adventure}: we hiked, kayaked and slept in tents.
questions.explain: Correct. An adventure is an exciting experience.

questions.sentence: I need to buy an {adventure} for my mom's birthday.
questions.explain: An adventure is an exciting experience. For a birthday, you buy a present.

questions.them: How was the trip to Eilat?? 🌊
questions.me: Amazing! We went diving with dolphins. What an {_}!

questions.them: Do you want to try the new escape room with us on Friday?
questions.me: Yes! I'm always up for a new {_} 😎

questions.sentence: My brother is very {_}: he wants to climb Mount Everest one day.
questions.hint: You need an adjective that describes a person. This one ends in -ous.

options.text: We had a real {adventure} in the jungle.
For me, every good book is an {adventure}.
The test was full of {adventures}: I got three questions wrong.
She's an {adventurous} cook who always tries new recipes.

questions.explain: An adventure is exciting (even in your imagination, like a book), and an adventurous person likes trying new things. Wrong answers on a test are mistakes, not adventures.

words.definition: feeling fear or worry about something

meet.sentence: My little sister is {afraid} of the dark, so she sleeps with the light on.

questions.prompt: feeling fear or worry about something

questions.sentence: Don't be {_}. The dog is friendly and won't bite you.
Many people are {afraid} of speaking in front of a big group.
questions.explain: Correct. You are afraid of something.

questions.sentence: This pizza is so {afraid}, I want another slice!
questions.explain: Afraid describes feeling fear. A pizza you love is tasty or delicious.

questions.them: Why didn't you go on the big roller coaster? 🎢
questions.me: Honestly? I was {_}! It's so high 😱

questions.them: Are you coming to the beach tonight?
questions.me: Maybe... I'm a bit {_} of swimming in the dark.

questions.sentence: I'm {_} we've sold all the tickets. Sorry!
questions.explain: 'I'm afraid…' is a polite way to give bad news.

words.definition: something you want to achieve; a goal

meet.sentence: The {aim} of the game is to score more points than the other team.

questions.prompt: something you want to achieve; a goal

questions.sentence: Our main {_} this year is to pass the English exam with a high grade.
The {aim} of the project is to clean up the beach.
questions.explain: Correct. An aim is something you want to achieve.

questions.sentence: I fell on the stairs and hurt my {aim}.
questions.explain: An aim is a goal. On the stairs, you could hurt your arm or your knee.

questions.them: Why are you running every day? 🏃‍♀️
questions.me: My {_} is to finish the Tel Aviv marathon in February!

questions.them: What's the point of this assignment?
questions.me: The teacher said the {_} is to practise writing emails.

questions.sentence: The new app is {_} at teenagers who want to learn to cook.
questions.explain: 'Aimed at' a group means made for that group.

words.definition: very surprising and very good

meet.sentence: The view from the top of the Azrieli Tower is {amazing}!

questions.prompt: very surprising and very good

questions.sentence: The singer has an {_} voice. Everyone stopped talking when she sang.
We had an {amazing} time at the concert last night.
questions.explain: Correct. Amazing = really great, surprising in a good way.

questions.sentence: I was so {amazing} before the test that I couldn't sleep.
questions.explain: Amazing describes something great. Before a test, you might feel nervous or worried.

questions.them: So? How was the new Pixar movie? 🍿
questions.me: Totally {_}! I cried and laughed at the same time.

questions.them: Did you try the new falafel place? 🧆
questions.me: Yes, it's {_}. Best falafel in the city!

questions.sentence: We were {_} when our teacher arrived at school on a horse.
questions.hint: You need an adjective for how people felt. Feelings often end in -ed.

options.text: It always {amazes} me how fast you learned to swim.
I'm {amazed} by her talent.
The movie was {amazed}.
What an {amazing} idea!

questions.explain: Things are amazing; people feel amazed. 'The movie was amazed' should be 'The movie was amazing'.

words.definition: how much there is of something

meet.sentence: Elephants eat a huge {amount} of food every day.

questions.prompt: how much there is of something

questions.sentence: You only need a small {_} of salt for this recipe.
The {amount} of homework this week is crazy!
questions.explain: Correct. Use amount with things you can't count, like homework, water or money.

questions.sentence: Let's meet at the {amount} near the bus stop.
questions.explain: Amount means how much there is of something. You meet at a place, like a café.

questions.them: How much did you spend on the trip? 💸
questions.me: A crazy {_} of money. I'm broke now 😅

questions.them: Why are you drinking so much water? 💧
questions.me: The coach said we need a large {_} of water when it's this hot.

questions.sentence: A large {_} of students came to the meeting.
questions.explain: Students can be counted, so use 'number'. Use 'amount' for things you can't count, like water or time.

words.definition: words that say you are sorry

meet.sentence: Shir sent me a long {apology} after she forgot my birthday.

questions.prompt: words that say you are sorry

questions.sentence: The bus company posted an {_} for the delays this morning.
I think you owe your sister an {apology}.
questions.explain: Correct. You owe someone an apology when you should say sorry.

questions.sentence: We ate a delicious chocolate {apology} for dessert.
questions.explain: An apology is saying sorry. For dessert, you might eat a chocolate cake.

questions.them: Are you still angry at Yoav? 😕
questions.me: Not really. He sent me an {_} and we're OK now.

questions.them: The teacher was really upset that we were late.
questions.me: Yeah, we should write her an {_} together.

questions.sentence: I want to {_} for what I said yesterday. I was wrong.
questions.hint: You need a verb that means 'say sorry'. It ends in -ize (or -ise).

questions.sentence: Please accept our {_} for any problems this may cause.
questions.explain: 'Please accept our apologies' is a formal way to say sorry, often in emails or announcements.

words.definition: free to use, buy, or talk to

meet.sentence: Sorry, there are no seats {available} on Friday's flight.

questions.prompt: free to use, buy, or talk to

questions.sentence: Is the doctor {_} today, or is she on vacation?
The new album is {available} on Spotify from today.
questions.explain: Correct. Available = you can get it or use it.

questions.sentence: My grandfather is very {available}: he's 95 years old.
questions.explain: Available means free to use or talk to. For someone who's 95, you'd say old.

questions.them: Can you help me with math homework this afternoon? 🙏
questions.me: Sure, I'm {_} after 4!

questions.them: Do they have the shoes in size 43?
questions.me: I checked online. Only size 42 is {_} 😕

questions.sentence: The free tickets are {_} only to students with a school ID.
questions.explain: 'Available to' someone means they can get it.

words.definition: to act in a certain way, especially in a good or polite way

meet.sentence: The children {behaved} very well during the long flight.

questions.prompt: to act in a certain way, especially in a good or polite way

questions.sentence: If you don't {_} in class, the teacher will call your parents.
Our dog {behaves} badly when we leave him alone.
questions.explain: Correct. You can behave well or badly.

questions.sentence: Can you {behave} me the salt, please?
questions.explain: Behave means to act in a certain way. At the table, you ask someone to pass the salt.

questions.them: Your little brother is coming to the party?? 😬
questions.me: Don't worry, I told him to {_} himself!

questions.them: Why did the teacher send Tomer out?
questions.me: He didn't {_} during the test. He kept talking 🙄

questions.sentence: The school has strict rules about students' {_} on trips.
questions.hint: You need a noun after students'. Behave → behav- + -ior (British: -iour).

options.text: {Behave} yourself at Grandma's house!
This car {behaves} well on wet roads.
She {behaved} the dishes after dinner.
Scientists study how bees {behave}.

questions.explain: Behave describes how people, animals and even machines act. After dinner, you wash the dishes.

words.definition: to look at how two or more things are the same or different

meet.sentence: Before buying a phone, I always {compare} prices on different websites.
options: look at them side by side

questions.prompt: to look at how two or more things are the same or different

questions.sentence: In your essay, {_} life in the city with life in a village.
Don't {compare} yourself to others. Everyone learns at their own speed.
questions.explain: Correct. Compare = look at what's the same and what's different.

questions.sentence: I {compared} a glass of water because I was thirsty.
questions.explain: Compare means to look at differences. When you're thirsty, you drink a glass of water.

questions.them: Which laptop should I buy? 🤔
questions.me: Let's {_} them. Send me both links!

questions.them: My mom always says my sister is better at math 😒
questions.me: That's annoying. Parents shouldn't {_} their kids.

questions.sentence: There's no {_} between homemade pizza and frozen pizza!
questions.hint: You need a noun. Compare → compar- + -ison.

questions.sentence: {_} to last year, this summer was much hotter.
questions.explain: 'Compared to…' shows a difference between two things.

words.definition: to try to win against other people

meet.sentence: Twenty schools will {compete} in the national robotics contest.

questions.prompt: to try to win against other people

questions.sentence: Our team will {_} against the best team in the country on Sunday.
Thousands of runners {competed} in the Jerusalem Marathon.
questions.explain: Correct. You compete in a race or a competition.

questions.sentence: I {competed} my homework at midnight.
questions.explain: Compete means to try to win. For homework, you'd say you finished it.

questions.them: Are you going to the chess tournament? ♟️
questions.me: Yes! I'm going to {_} for the first time 😬

questions.them: Why are you training so hard?
questions.me: I want to {_} in the national swimming championship!

questions.sentence: Our class won first prize in the photo {_}!
questions.hint: You need a noun. Many nouns end in -tion.

questions.sentence: My brother is very {_}: he hates losing, even at board games.
questions.explain: You need an adjective that describes a person: competitive.

words.definition: to make someone believe something or agree to do something

meet.sentence: I finally {convinced} my parents to let me go to the concert.

questions.prompt: to make someone believe something or agree to do something

questions.sentence: Can you help me {_} my dad to buy a dog?
Her speech {convinced} everyone to vote for her.
questions.explain: Correct. You convince someone to do something.

questions.sentence: We {convinced} a cake for Dad's birthday.
questions.explain: Convince means to make someone agree. For a birthday, you bake a cake.

questions.them: Is your mom letting you come to Eilat with us? 🏖️
questions.me: Not yet... I'm trying to {_} her! 🙏

questions.them: Why did you join the drama club? You hate acting 😂
questions.me: Shira {_} me. She said it would be fun!

questions.sentence: I'm {_} that we'll win the game tomorrow.
questions.hint: You need an adjective that means 'very sure'. It looks like a past form.

options.text: It's hard to {convince} teenagers to sleep early.
She wasn't {convinced} by his story.
He {convinced} the ball into the goal.
They tried to {convince} me, but I still said no.

questions.explain: You convince people (to do something, or that something is true), and you can be convinced or not. You kick a ball into a goal.

words.definition: the chance that something bad or harmful will happen

meet.sentence: The sign said: "{Danger}! Deep water. No swimming."

questions.prompt: the chance that something bad or harmful will happen

questions.sentence: The doctors said the patient is out of {_} and will go home soon.
Climbing without a rope can put your life in {danger}.
questions.explain: Correct. Your life can be in danger.

questions.sentence: I love the {danger} in this soup. It's so spicy!
questions.explain: Danger is the chance of something bad. For soup, you'd talk about the taste.

questions.them: Is it OK to swim at that beach? There's no lifeguard 🌊
questions.me: No way! The waves are a real {_} there.

questions.them: Why did they close the old bridge?
questions.me: It's falling apart. It's a {_} to everyone who walks on it.

questions.sentence: Texting while driving is really {_}.
questions.hint: You need an adjective after 'really'. Add -ous.

questions.sentence: Some animals, like the white rhino, are in {_} of disappearing forever.
questions.explain: 'In danger of' + -ing means something bad might happen.

words.definition: to damage something so badly that it can't be used or fixed

meet.sentence: The fire {destroyed} three houses, but everyone got out safely.

questions.prompt: to damage something so badly that it can't be used or fixed

questions.sentence: The storm {_} the farmers' fields, so there were no vegetables that summer.
Plastic in the sea can {destroy} the homes of many fish.
questions.explain: Correct. Destroy = damage so badly it can't be used anymore.

questions.sentence: I {destroyed} my friend at the bus stop and said hi.
questions.explain: Destroy means to damage something completely. At the bus stop, you met your friend.

questions.them: What happened to your phone?! 📱
questions.me: My little brother dropped it in the pool. It's totally {_} 😭

questions.them: Did you see the sand castle we built? 🏰
questions.me: Yes, but the waves are going to {_} it soon 😅

questions.sentence: The earthquake caused terrible {_} in the city.
questions.hint: You need a noun. Destroy → destruct- + -ion.

options.text: The injury {destroyed} his hopes of playing in the final.
Hackers {destroyed} the school's website.
She {destroyed} a new language in one year.
Too much sugar can {destroy} your teeth.

questions.explain: You can destroy things, and even hopes or plans. A new language is something you learn.

words.definition: a problem; something that is hard to do or understand

meet.sentence: I had some {difficulty} finding the classroom on my first day.

questions.prompt: a problem; something that is hard to do or understand

questions.sentence: My grandmother has {_} walking, so she uses a stick.
Many students have {difficulty} with English spelling.
questions.explain: Correct. You have difficulty with something, or difficulty doing something.

questions.sentence: I put the {difficulty} in the fridge so it stays cold.
questions.explain: A difficulty is a problem. In the fridge, you put food or drinks.

questions.them: Did you finish the physics homework? 🤯
questions.me: Almost. I had some {_} with the last question.

questions.them: How's your new school?
questions.me: Good! I had {_} making friends at first, but now it's fine 😊

questions.sentence: The test was so {_} that half the class failed.
questions.hint: You need an adjective. Take off the -y.

questions.sentence: We had a few {_} on the trip, but we got home safely.
questions.explain: Here difficulties means problems. It's countable: one difficulty, two difficulties.

words.definition: to go somewhere where you can't be seen or found

meet.sentence: The cat {disappeared} for two days, and then came home hungry.

questions.prompt: to go somewhere where you can't be seen or found

questions.sentence: The sun {_} behind the clouds, and it started to rain.
My keys always {disappear} when I'm in a hurry!
questions.explain: Correct. Things disappear when you can't find them.

questions.sentence: Let's {disappear} a movie tonight.
questions.explain: Disappear means to go out of sight. With a movie, you watch it.

questions.them: Where are the cookies I baked? 🍪
questions.me: Ha! They {_} in ten minutes. Everyone loved them!

questions.them: Is your bike still outside your building?
questions.me: No! It {_} last night. I think someone stole it 😡

questions.sentence: The police are investigating the {_} of a famous painting from the museum.
questions.hint: You need a noun after 'the'. Add -ance.

questions.sentence: Many old traditions are slowly {_} because young people don't follow them anymore.
questions.explain: Things can slowly disappear, meaning stop existing: disappearing.

words.definition: to find something, or learn something, for the first time

meet.sentence: Scientists {discovered} a new kind of fish near Eilat.

questions.prompt: to find something, or learn something, for the first time

questions.sentence: When I opened the box, I {_} that it was empty.
On the trip, we {discovered} a small waterfall hidden behind the trees.
questions.explain: Correct. You discover something you didn't know was there.

questions.sentence: I {discovered} my teeth before bed.
questions.explain: Discover means to find something new. Before bed, you brush your teeth.

questions.them: How did you find this amazing café? ☕
questions.me: I {_} it by accident when I got lost in Jaffa!

questions.them: Why do you love that band so much? 🎸
questions.me: I {_} their music last summer, and now I listen every day.

questions.sentence: The {_} of penicillin saved millions of lives.
questions.hint: You need a noun. Discover → discover + -y.

options.text: Scientists {discovered} water on Mars.
I {discovered} that I'm good at drawing.
She {discovered} the window to let in some air.
Kids love to {discover} new places.

questions.explain: You discover places, facts and even things about yourself. To let in air, you open the window.
